lines.say: Chapter one. Hit the numbers.

Before WorldCom, Ebbers had been a teacher, a coach and a motel operator. In nineteen eighty-three he invested in a small long-distance company in Mississippi. By two thousand, renamed WorldCom, it had about ninety thousand employees in sixty-five countries, and reported revenues of thirty-nine billion dollars.
lines.show: Before WorldCom, Ebbers had been a teacher, a coach and a motel operator. In 1983 he invested in a small long-distance company in Mississippi. By 2000, renamed WorldCom, it had about 90,000 employees in 65 countries, and reported revenues of $39 billion.

scene.label: in reported revenues —|90,000 employees in 65 countries
scene.src: U.S. v. Ebbers, 458 F.3d 110 (2d Cir. Jul 28, 2006)

lines.say: Its largest expense was something called line costs: the fees it paid to use other companies' telephone networks.

scene.title: “line costs”
scene.src: Brief for the United States in Opposition, Ebbers v. United States, No. 06-590 (2007)

lines.say: Then the dot-com bubble burst. Demand fell. In the third quarter of two thousand, line costs came in almost one billion dollars higher than expected.
lines.show: Then the dot-com bubble burst. Demand fell. In the third quarter of 2000, line costs came in almost $1 billion higher than expected.

scene.title: “almost $1 billion higher than expected”
scene.src: Brief for the United States in Opposition, Ebbers v. United States, No. 06-590 (2007)

lines.say: Ebbers had his own reasons to watch the stock. He had borrowed over four hundred million dollars from banks, using his WorldCom shares as collateral. As the price fell, the margin calls came, and in October two thousand, WorldCom took on the liability for his bank debts. He now owed that money to WorldCom instead.
lines.show: Ebbers had his own reasons to watch the stock. He had borrowed over $400 million from banks, using his WorldCom shares as collateral. As the price fell, the margin calls came, and in October 2000, WorldCom took on the liability for his bank debts. He now owed that money to WorldCom instead.

scene.src: U.S. v. Ebbers, 458 F.3d 110 (2d Cir. Jul 28, 2006)

lines.say: According to the trial evidence, as the appeals court described it, chief financial officer Scott Sullivan told Ebbers they should issue an earnings warning. Ebbers refused. When Sullivan said meeting expectations would take an improper adjustment, Ebbers replied:

scene.src: U.S. v. Ebbers, 458 F.3d 110 (2d Cir. Jul 28, 2006)

lines.say: We have to hit our numbers.

lines.say: Chapter two. The line costs.

The first line-cost fix came from reserves. On Sullivan's instructions, Controller David Myers and his staff reduced line-cost accounts and drew down reserves by the same amounts. Reported line costs fell by about eight hundred twenty-eight million dollars.
lines.show: The first line-cost fix came from reserves. On Sullivan's instructions, Controller David Myers and his staff reduced line-cost accounts and drew down reserves by the same amounts. Reported line costs fell by about $828 million.

scene.kicker: THIRD QUARTER 2000 · PER THE APPEALS COURT
scene.src: U.S. v. Ebbers, 458 F.3d 110 (2d Cir. Jul 28, 2006)

lines.say: Two accountants on that staff believed the entries were wrong and considered resigning. Told about it, Ebbers said they shouldn't be putting people in this position, and apologized to Myers.

scene.title: “considered resigning”
scene.src: U.S. v. Ebbers, 458 F.3d 110 (2d Cir. Jul 28, 2006)

lines.say: The next quarter, the staff cut the income tax reserve by four hundred seven million dollars and altered other accounts, until reported line costs were seven hundred ninety-seven million dollars lower. The monthly reports sent to Ebbers carried the reduced line costs: an apparent gross margin of seventy-eight percent in September two thousand, and seventy-four percent in December. WorldCom had never achieved margins like that.
lines.show: The next quarter, the staff cut the income tax reserve by $407 million and altered other accounts, until reported line costs were $797 million lower. The monthly reports sent to Ebbers carried the reduced line costs: an apparent gross margin of 78% in September 2000, and 74% in December. WorldCom had never achieved margins like that.

scene.src: U.S. v. Ebbers, 458 F.3d 110 (2d Cir. Jul 28, 2006)

lines.say: By early two thousand one, the reserves were largely exhausted. Sullivan proposed something new. Line costs had always been operating expenses. Now part of them would be booked as capital expenditures, like investments in equipment.
lines.show: By early 2001, the reserves were largely exhausted. Sullivan proposed something new. Line costs had always been operating expenses. Now part of them would be booked as capital expenditures, like investments in equipment.

lines.say: Chapter three. The audit.

In March two thousand two, the S.E.C. began to investigate WorldCom. At the end of April, the board asked Ebbers to resign. He did, on April twenty-ninth. In May, he bought three million more shares of WorldCom stock.

lines.say: A month after he left, WorldCom's own internal audit department found the capitalized line costs. TIME magazine later reported that its head, Cynthia Cooper, and her team worked late into the night, keeping the project secret.

Its complaint said WorldCom had overstated its income by about three point oh five five billion dollars in two thousand one, and seven hundred ninety-seven million in early two thousand two. For two thousand one, it said, the company had actually lost about six hundred sixty-two million dollars.

lines.say: Chapter four. The trial.

Myers and three former members of his department were convicted. On March second, two thousand four, Sullivan pleaded guilty and agreed to cooperate. That same day, an indictment against Ebbers was unsealed. That September, a superseding indictment charged him with nine counts.
